771.title: Egeria's diary
771.hook: a woman traveled to the Holy Land and wrote down how Jerusalem kept Holy Week
771.howItsDone: Christians make pilgrimages to Jerusalem, Rome, Santiago de Compostela and other holy places, and some churches walk in procession with palms on Palm Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicholas of Myra, and your line was a gift by night. Did your gift go out without your name on it? Day seven hundred seventy-one.

Dear sisters. That's who she's writing to: a circle of women back home, somewhere in the west, who can't make the trip. So she makes it for them, and writes it all down. Her name, as it reaches us, is Egeria. She travels through the lands of the Bible, climbs mountains, asks the local monks and clergy to show her the places where the stories happened, and reads the passage aloud on the spot. Then she gets to Jerusalem, and she does something even more useful. She writes down, day by day, how the church there keeps Holy Week, the days before Easter. She's a traveler with a notebook. And because of her, we can stand in that crowd. Today's word is what she was doing.

Palm Sunday first. Egeria describes the people gathering with their bishop on the Mount of Olives, then walking down into the city together, everyone carrying branches of palm or olive. Children too small to walk ride on their parents' shoulders. And all the way down, they sing the line the crowds sang for Jesus: "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." They aren't just remembering the story. They're walking it, on the same hill. That's pilgrimage: a journey to a holy place, where the walking itself becomes a prayer. Now Good Friday, and a startling detail. Egeria says the bishop sits with the wood of the cross on a table in front of him, held in his hands, with deacons standing around. The people come forward one by one, bow, touch it with their forehead and eyes, and kiss it. And the deacons guard it closely, she explains, because once someone bit off a piece and ran off with it. That's in her diary. Holiness and human nature, side by side. One more thing she noticed. The bishop preaches in Greek. But not everyone in the crowd understands Greek, so a priest stands beside him and translates into Syriac, and others explain it for those who speak Latin. A crowd from everywhere, in one week, in one city, each hearing it in their own words. A psalm about going up to Jerusalem begins, "I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD." Egeria went, and she wrote it down so her sisters could walk where she walked, without leaving home.
screen: `PALM SUNDAY: DOWN THE MOUNT OF OLIVES.`
`LET US GO INTO THE HOUSE OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be Egeria for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place that mattered to you: a church, a grandmother's kitchen, a hospital corridor, a beach, a street you walked on a hard day. Go back there slowly. What did you see first? What did you hear? Who was there? Now find one small detail you'd almost forgotten, the kind Egeria wrote down. After the bell, if you like, start a travel journal with that one place and that one detail, for someone who couldn't be there. The bell holds the time.
Pilgrimage. A journey to a holy place, where the walking itself becomes a kind of prayer, and where, for Egeria, the story was read aloud on the very spot.
Your line: walk where they walked. Today, walk somewhere on purpose, even a short block, and write down one detail for someone who wasn't there. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

772.title: Pachomius' community
772.hook: monks living together under a rule: work, prayer, shared bread
772.howItsDone: Christian monks and nuns in Orthodox, Catholic and other traditions live in community under a rule, sharing work, prayer at set hours, and meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Egeria's diary, pilgrimage, and your line was walk where they walked. What one detail did you write down for someone who wasn't there? Day seven hundred seventy-two.

Locked up with other recruits in a city on the Nile, rounded up for the emperor's army, sits a young man who isn't a Christian. He's hungry and far from home. And in the evening, strangers come with food and drink for the prisoners. He asks who they are. Christians, he's told: people who are kind to strangers, for the sake of the God of heaven. His name is Pachomius. The Life written about him says that night he promised that, if he got free, he would spend his life serving others. A few days ago we met Antony, who walked out alone into the desert. Pachomius goes into the desert too. But he doesn't stay alone.

After his release, Pachomius is baptized and learns the hard life of a hermit from an old monk. Then, at a deserted village by the river called Tabennesi, the story goes, he's told to build a place where many could live together. So he does. Then it gets hard. The Life says his first followers took advantage of him. He served them, cooked for them, did the chores, and they treated him like the help. Eventually he gave them a rule, and when they wouldn't keep it, he sent them away. Living together turned out to be harder than living alone. So Pachomius organized it. Monks lived in houses, each with a leader. They worked with their hands, weaving mats and baskets, and the work supported the community and the poor. They gathered to pray at set times. They ate together, the same food, at a shared table. The sick were cared for. Nobody owned anything privately. People kept coming, and more communities were founded along the river. The book of Acts had already described this way of life, in the first Christians in Jerusalem: "they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." The Greek word behind fellowship there is koinonia, a sharing, a life held in common. And Pachomius' communities came to be called by that same name: the Koinonia. Here's the idea at its plainest. Alone in a cave, nobody leaves dishes in your sink. Nobody snores. Nobody needs you when you're tired. In community, everyone does. As the Life tells it, for Pachomius that was the point.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you share space or work with: a household, roommates, a team, a congregation. Notice the small friction points. The dishes. The trash. The one who's always late, or the one who always has to fix things. Don't stew. Just notice. Now pick one chore that usually falls to one person, and imagine doing it alongside them, not instead of them. Folding the laundry together. Clearing the table side by side. Pachomius' monks shared the work and the bread. If you pray, you can pray for the people you live with, by name. The bell holds the time.
Pachomius' community. The shared life Pachomius built by the Nile: houses of monks under a rule, with work, prayer and bread held in common.
Your line: together is harder, and better. Today, share one chore with someone, side by side, and stay until it's done. Day seven hundred seventy-two.

773.title: Basil's new city
773.hook: Basil of Caesarea built a place of care for the poor and sick, and his friend called it a new city
773.howItsDone: Churches and Christian orders run hospitals, clinics, hospices, shelters and food banks, and church members give to and volunteer in them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pachomius' community, and your line was together is harder, and better. Which chore did you share, and did you stay until it was done? Day seven hundred seventy-three.

"I will pull down my barns, and build greater." That's the rich man in one of Jesus' parables, in Luke's Gospel. His harvest is huge, so he plans bigger storage, and that night his life is asked of him. A man named Basil, then a priest in Caesarea, in what's now central Turkey, and later its bishop, preached on that line to his own people. And in his time, a famine came to his city. The rich of the city, like the man in the parable, had full barns. Basil had a sermon, a pulpit, and a gift for making people uncomfortable. What he did with them is today's story, and by the end he's built something on the edge of town that his close friend would call a new city.

The famine comes first. His friend Gregory tells it, in a speech in Basil's memory. Basil opened the storehouses of those who had them, by the force of his preaching. He gathered the hungry in one place, and he didn't just organize it. He served them himself, with his own hands, alongside his helpers. In his sermon on the barns, Basil pushes hard. In paraphrase: the bread you keep in store belongs to the hungry; the coat in your closet belongs to the one without one. He isn't asking for leftovers. He's asking whose the extra really is. Then he builds. Outside Caesarea, Basil put up a whole complex: lodging for travelers and strangers, a place for the poor, care for the sick, with people to nurse them and workers to keep it going. A local governor was apparently uneasy about it. Basil wrote to him: what harm does this do the state? We're housing strangers and caring for the sick. Gregory's speech describes it with real wonder. Go a little way out of the city, he says in paraphrase, and look at the new city, a storehouse of devotion, where the rich put their surplus. And he singles out the people others avoided: those with the disease that disfigured skin and drove sufferers out of town. Basil, Gregory says, didn't keep his distance. He greeted them, embraced them, even kissed them, as brothers. That's the image to keep. Not a building, but a bishop bending down to kiss someone everyone else had sent away. A city of mercy, built just outside the city.
screen: `THE FAMINE: HE SERVED WITH HIS HANDS.`
`THE BREAD YOU KEEP IS THE HUNGRY'S.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a place near you where people are cared for when they're sick or poor. A hospital, a free clinic, a hospice, a shelter, a food bank. If you've ever been carried by one, remember that. Picture the people who work there tonight, in the late hours. Basil asked his governor what harm the place did. Ask the opposite: what does this place run short of? Blankets, cans, a driver, a thank-you for the night staff. Choose one small gift you could actually give it. If you pray, you can pray for the people inside, the sick and the ones who care for them. The bell holds the time.
Basil's new city. The place of care Basil of Caesarea built outside his town, for strangers, the poor and the sick, that his friend Gregory called a new city.
Your line: a city of mercy. Today, give the gift you chose to a hospital, clinic, shelter or food bank, even if it's small. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

774.title: Gregory of Nazianzus
774.hook: a shy poet-bishop who preached on the Trinity in a tiny church and resigned rather than fight
774.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians honor Gregory as a teacher of the faith, calling him the Theologian, and Catholic and other churches keep his feast; his sermons on God are still read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Basil's new city, and your line was a city of mercy. Where did your small gift go? Day seven hundred seventy-four.

Yesterday, a friend's speech in Basil's memory told us about the new city. That friend is today's word. Gregory, from a small town called Nazianzus. He and Basil met as students in Athens, and in that speech Gregory remembers it: two young men who knew only two roads, one to church, one to their teachers. Gregory loved books, quiet and poetry. What he didn't love was being in charge. When his own father, a bishop, made him a priest, Gregory ran away to think it over, and later wrote a long defense of why he'd fled. And yet this reluctant man was about to be sent into the middle of a fierce religious argument in the empire's new capital.

The capital was Constantinople, and the argument was the one we met at Nicaea, still raging. In that city, the people holding to the Nicene creed were few, and had lost their churches. So Gregory preached in a small house chapel, given by a relative. He named it Anastasia: resurrection. A small room, standing for a faith he hoped would rise again. And there he preached a series of sermons on God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. They're careful, and they're humble. He keeps saying that talking about God is dangerous, that God is beyond our words, and that the way to know God is by living a clean, prayerful life, not by winning debates. Later tradition gave him a title: Gregory the Theologian. Then the tide turned. A new emperor favored the Nicene side, the great churches were handed back, and Gregory, the shy poet, was put in charge of the city's church. At the council held there, he presided for a time. And then the fights began, about him. Rival bishops said his appointment broke the rules. Factions formed. Gregory looked at it and, by his own account, reached for the prophet Jonah, who told the sailors in the storm: "Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you." He resigned. He went home to Cappadocia, wrote poems, including a long one about his own life, and cared for a small flock. He didn't keep the job. He chose the calm over the chair.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Think of a fight you're in, or about to be in, that doesn't really need to happen. A group chat, a family argument, a meeting, a comment thread. Something where being right has started to matter more than anything you're actually defending. Picture it like a boat in a storm. Ask: if I stepped back from this one, what would actually be lost? Sometimes the answer is: something real. Then stay. But sometimes the answer is: only my position. If you pray, you can bring that fight to God and leave it there for now. The bell holds the time.
Gregory of Nazianzus. Basil's friend, a poet and preacher on the Trinity, who led the church in Constantinople and stepped down rather than keep a fight going.
Your line: peace over position. Today, in the needless fight you named, step back once, out loud: I'll let this one go. Day seven hundred seventy-four.

775.title: Macrina
775.hook: the older sister who taught her brothers Basil and Gregory, and led a community at home
775.howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor Macrina as a saint, and Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina and his dialogue with her are read as spiritual classics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory of Nazianzus, and your line was peace over position. Did you step back from the fight you named? Day seven hundred seventy-five.

A heads-up about names. Yesterday's Gregory was Basil's friend from Nazianzus. Today there's another Gregory: Basil's younger brother, Gregory of Nyssa, also a bishop, also a deep writer. And both of those brothers had an older sister. Her name was Macrina. She never became a bishop. She didn't preach at councils. And yet her brother Gregory wrote her life, and wrote a whole book of conversation with her, and in it he hardly ever calls her by her name. He calls her the Teacher.

Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Macrina tells it from the start. She was the eldest child. As a girl, she was engaged to a young man who died before the wedding. Her family wanted to arrange another match. She refused. In her view, Gregory says, she was still promised to him, a man alive to God, and she would wait for the resurrection. So she stayed home with her mother and the younger children. Then Basil came home from his studies. And here Gregory is startlingly frank about his famous brother. In paraphrase: Basil came back excessively proud of his skill as a speaker, looking down on everyone important in town. Macrina took him in hand. She drew him, Gregory says, toward a simpler life, away from fame, toward God. The Basil we met two days ago, kissing the sick outside his new city, had a sister behind him. Then Macrina turned her household into a community. She persuaded her mother to live on equal terms with the women who had been their servants: the same table, the same work, the same prayers. Rank dissolved around the dinner table. She also raised and taught her youngest brother, Peter, who became a bishop too. At the end of her life, Gregory came to see her, heavy with grief after Basil's death. She was dying, and she comforted him, and the two of them talked about the soul and the resurrection. He wrote it down as a dialogue, with her as the Teacher, and himself as the student who keeps asking questions. The teacher of teachers: a woman at home, teaching brothers who would go on to teach the church.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who was a Macrina for you. An older sister, maybe, or a cousin, an aunt, a neighbor, a coach, a coworker who showed you the ropes. Someone who taught you without a title, maybe even took you down a peg when you needed it. Let one person come. Remember one specific thing they did or said. Hold it. If you pray, you can thank God for them, by name. Then think of how you might thank them directly: a message, a call, a note. The bell holds the time.
Macrina. The older sister of Basil and Gregory of Nyssa, who drew her brothers toward God and led a community at home, and whom Gregory called the Teacher.
Your line: the teacher of teachers. Today, send the person you named a thank-you that mentions the one specific thing. Day seven hundred seventy-five.

776.title: Constantinople (381)
776.hook: the council completes the creed: the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life
776.carry: the lord, the giver of life
776.howItsDone: Christians in Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed together in worship, Orthodox churches without the words and the Son, most Western churches with them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Macrina, and your line was the teacher of teachers. Did your thank-you reach the person you named? Day seven hundred seventy-six.

The creed from Nicaea spent a long time on the Son. Begotten, not made. Of one substance with the Father. Then it reached the Holy Spirit, and said, in effect, just this: and in the Holy Spirit. Full stop. One short line. For a while that seemed enough. Then people started asking the same kind of question about the Spirit that Arius had asked about the Son. Is the Spirit God, or a power God sends, or something God made? So bishops gathered again, this time in Constantinople, the city that carried Constantine's name, the city where Gregory had preached in his small chapel and then stepped down. What they added is still said in churches.
screen: `NICAEA: AND IN THE HOLY SPIRIT. FULL STOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the fuller creed, the form that came out of Constantinople, in the old English of the Book of Common Prayer. On the Spirit, it now says: "And I believe in the Holy Ghost, The Lord and giver of life." Two titles. First, Lord: the same word the creed uses for Jesus, a title that belongs to God. Second, giver of life. In the Greek, that's one word, zoopoion, the life-maker. Some readers hear in it the second chapter of Genesis, where God forms the first human from the dust and "breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." And Jesus in John's Gospel: "It is the spirit that quickeneth." Quickeneth: makes alive. Then the creed goes on, and the next line is where churches today differ, so it's worth saying plainly. The council's Greek says the Spirit proceeds from the Father. Later, in the West, the words and the Son were added, and the Prayer Book text has them. Orthodox Christians say the creed without those words. In the West, Catholic Christians, and Protestant churches that use the creed, generally say it with them. That phrase has been argued over for a long time. Then the creed adds: "Who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, Who spake by the Prophets." Worshipped together: not a lesser helper but one God, Father, Son and Spirit. This creed is the one later called, simply, the Nicene Creed. So the creed said in churches on Sunday carries both councils in it, and its closing section, on the Spirit, runs on to the church, baptism and the life to come.
screen: `THE LORD: A TITLE THAT BELONGS TO GOD.`
`THE GIVER OF LIFE: BREATH IN THE DUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and let your breathing slow. Notice the breath coming in, without forcing it. Genesis pictures life starting with a breath. So let each breath in be the words giver of, and each breath out, life. Giver of. Life. If you pray, you can say the creed's line silently instead: the Lord, and giver of life. If you don't, simply notice the breath arriving on its own, without your making it. Stay with that for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Constantinople. Constantine's city, where bishops met again and completed the creed's words on the Holy Spirit: the Lord, the giver of life.
Your line: the lord, the giver of life. Today, three times, stop and take one slow breath, and notice it as given. Day seven hundred seventy-six.

777.title: Ambrose and the emperor
777.hook: after a massacre, Bishop Ambrose makes Emperor Theodosius do public penance
777.howItsDone: Christians remember Ambrose as a saint and a bishop of Milan; the story of Theodosius' penance is retold as an example of repentance and of a pastor's courage before power.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantinople, and the creed's words for the Spirit. Your line was the lord, the giver of life. Where did you notice life being given? Day seven hundred seventy-seven.

A city has just been punished by its own emperor. In Thessalonica, after a riot, Emperor Theodosius orders a reprisal, and soldiers kill the people gathered in the city's circus. The old historians say the guilty and the innocent died together. The emperor is a baptized Christian. His bishop, up in Milan, is a man named Ambrose, and he has known the emperor well. Now Ambrose has to decide what a bishop does when a man with that much power has blood on his hands. Today: Ambrose and the emperor.

We have two kinds of evidence, and they tell it differently. The first is a letter from Ambrose himself to Theodosius. It is careful, almost tender. Ambrose says he has written it in his own hand, so that the emperor alone will read it. He says he cannot offer the sacrifice of the altar with the emperor present, not until he repents. And he reminds him of King David. David also sinned terribly, and the prophet Nathan came and told him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb. David burned with anger at the rich man, until Nathan said, in the King James words, "Thou art the man." David confessed. Ambrose's point is that a king who repents is not made smaller by it. The second account comes from a historian, Theodoret. His version is a scene. The emperor arrives at the church in Milan, and Ambrose meets him at the door and will not let him in. Theodosius says that David sinned too. Ambrose answers: you followed him in sinning, now follow him in repenting. Readers handle Theodoret's drama with care; the letter is quieter. But the sources agree on what came next. The emperor did public penance before the people, and only then was received back to communion. Ambrose spoke of it at the emperor's funeral: Theodosius took off the signs of his royalty and wept for his sin in church. Just days ago on this path, an emperor's favor turned the church from hunted to favored. Here is the edge of that favor. Ambrose was no rebel. Still, he would not pretend. And notice the manner: he wrote alone first, and left a door open. Readers draw different lessons from it. Some see the church standing over the throne, others a conscience standing before a ruler. Both start from Nathan's line.
screen: `A PRIVATE LETTER, IN HIS OWN HAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a powerful person to account, kindly. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come: someone with power over others whose choice troubles you: a boss, a leader, a public figure, maybe someone in your own family. If anger comes, set it down beside you for a moment. Then ask what Ambrose seems to have asked: what would a true word sound like, said privately, with a door left open? You don't have to send anything. Just find the sentence. If you pray, you can hold that person before God, by name. If you don't, hold them in plain attention for this minute. The bell holds the time.

Ambrose and the emperor: a bishop who said no, first in a letter, and a ruler who set aside the signs of his royalty to repent. That ends a week of a pilgrim, monks, a city of mercy, a poet, a teacher, and a creed.
Your line: no one is above it. Today, if you owe someone an apology, especially someone with less power than you, say it plainly, and don't dress it up. Day seven hundred seventy-seven.
